articles.title: Shock Picture of Asteroid NASA Smashed Reveal Stadium-Sized Scar
articles.description: The first images of an asteroid that NASA plowed a space probe into have been revealed. The DART satellite was launched in 2022 to strike the asteroid Dimorphos, with the collision occurring that December. The aim was to establish whether an asteroid hypothetically on a collision course with Earth could be knocked onto a different trajectory. A follow-up spacecraft, Hera, was launched by the European Space Agency to assess the damage. Dimorphos was not on a collision course with Earth. It was in the orbit of another, larger asteroid called Didymos. Hera confirmed that it had altered its orbit. “Much to our surprise, the answer turns out to be all three at once. The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid’s entire width,” said Hera‘s principal investigator, Patrick Michel. “NASA’s DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid’s orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself,” said the Hera mission manager, Ian Carnelli of the ESA. “By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.” Read it at The Guardian Read more at The Daily Beast.

articles.title: How Engineers Designed a Mission to One of Jupiter’s Icy Moons
articles.description: On 3 December 2026, a 30.5-meter-wide space probe will slingshot past Earth, picking up the speed it needs to reach Jupiter in 2030. The Europa Clipper is designed to investigate Jupiter’s enigmatic moon Europa and look for places that could support life in the ocean beneath the moon’s thick shell of ice. Tim Larson is the project manager for the mission at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and he spoke to IEEE Spectrum about designing and flying the Europa Clipper. Tim Larson Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years. Why take such a roundabout route to Jupiter? Tim Larson: That’s all driven by the energy that we got from our launch vehicle, the Falcon Heavy. It set a MEGA trajectory: Mars-Earth Gravity Assist. So about 4 months after launch, we flew by Mars, got an assist there. Now we’re coming back in for a final assist from Earth to get on our outbound trajectory to Jupiter. The Europa Clipper is set to orbit Jupiter and fly by Europa about 50 times to study it. Why not just orbit it directly? Larson: The big challenge is the radiation environment. It is so intense that any spacecraft orbiting Europa wouldn’t last very long. So the mission designers came through with this concept of the flybys. We will be in a three-week orbit around Jupiter, but the orbit is synchronized so that every time we fly by Jupiter, Europa is right there. Over time, you build up the coverage of the surface that we’re ultimately after. We spend a relatively short time in the high-radiation environment, and then the rest of the orbit is in a more benign environment where we can relay data back down to Earth, et cetera. The Europa Clipper relies on solar panels to generate power. Why not use a compact radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG)? Larson: It’s a national policy to only use RTGs if it is absolutely essential. A lot of the early concepts that focused on orbiting Europa had to go with RTG approaches, because you’d spend so much time in the shadow of Jupiter. Once we shifted over to the flyby mission approach, it turned out solar arrays would be feasible. How are Europa Clipper’s electronics different from other probes? Larson: One of the things that we dealt with in our design was the level of radiation tolerance that we had to get in all our parts. In our main avionics module—we call it the vault—everything in there is designed to an exposure of 150 kilorads (1,500 sieverts). To get our usual factor-of-two margin, we were buying parts that rated to 300 kilorads. That brings up side challenges, because when you buy high-radiation-tolerance versions of parts, you can’t always get the exact same part functionality. You might have to change your circuits a little bit. And they don’t always have the same form factor, so you have to accommodate that. How do you preserve fine-grained technical knowledge about the spacecraft over its yearslong mission lifetime? Larson: By the time we launch, we try to get everything documented. As we learn about the idiosyncrasies of the spacecraft, we capture that in databases. When we have personnel turnover, we try to have a lot of overlap. We’re looking at how AI can take in this broad array of information we have in multiple different formats and locations, and extract information. This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “Tim Larson.”

articles.title: NASA deliberately crashed into an asteroid. Now scientists are surveying the damage.
articles.description: A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash. In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course. The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday. The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet. "Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission. The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide. The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact. It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space. The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid. Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes. But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions. "Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel. "The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid." The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too. The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid. A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was. This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth. "It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team. "We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'." Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet. The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city. "We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions. "The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there." She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth. "The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added. "But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that." Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us. A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor. There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long. Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029. But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface. This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close. Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).
